- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.

- The pokeball is a CSS `background-image` on `#workspaces:not(.taskbar) button.active` in `style.css`. There is exactly one `.active` button per bar as Waybar sees it, but with `all-outputs: true` all bars agree on the same globally focused workspace.

# Waybar Hyprland Workspaces Module: Key Configuration Details

## (1) The "all-outputs" Option

When set to **false** (default), workspaces display only on their assigned output/monitor. When set to **true**, "all workspace groups are shown" across the entire bar regardless of assignment.

## (2) CSS Classes for Workspace Buttons

The documentation lists these classes:
- `.active` — applied to the currently focused workspace
- `.empty` — non-active, non-special empty persistent workspaces
- `.visible` — workspaces visible but not active (useful for showing workspaces on other monitors)
- `.persistent` — non-empty persistent workspaces
- `.special` — non-active special workspaces
- `.urgent` — non-active urgent workspaces

Regarding active class scope: the documentation states "Will be shown, when workspace is active" without distinguishing per-monitor versus global application. However, the `all-outputs` setting controls whether you see workspaces from other monitors, suggesting that `.active` reflects the globally focused workspace (single focus point in Hyprland), while `.visible` captures workspaces active on other monitors.

## (3) Persistent Workspaces Format

This option "lists workspaces that should always be shown, even when they do not exist." Format uses an object where keys are workspace names and values are arrays of monitor names. The special `"*"` key applies defaults to all monitors. Example:

```
"*": [2,3,4,5]  // workspaces 2-5 on every monitor
"HDMI-A-1": [1] // only workspace 1 on that specific monitor
```

Note: these must also be declared persistent in your Hyprland config.

lastPrompt: Ok so I need to you to update the pokeball on the waybar on different monitors differently. Remember Hyprland allows a workspace to only exist on 1 monitor. Now let's see an example, if workspace 1 on…

aiTitle: Configure waybar pokeball per monitor in Hyprland

content.text:
I have a clear picture now. One key design decision determines the plan, so let me confirm it with you.

Here's the situation: the pokeball is pure CSS painted on the `.active` workspace button. Right now `hyprland/workspaces` has `"all-outputs": true`, so **both** monitors' bars render an identical workspace list and both highlight the single globally-focused workspace — which is exactly why both pokeballs jump together.

The only way Waybar can make one bar differ from another is `"all-outputs": false`, which filters each bar to **its own monitor's workspaces**. That cleanly gives one independent pokeball per monitor. The tradeoff: each bar then shows only that monitor's workspaces, not a shared list of all 9.

questions.question: With a per-monitor pokeball, how should each bar list workspaces? (This is the core tradeoff — Waybar can only differentiate bars by filtering to each monitor's own workspaces.)

options.label: Only that monitor's
options.description: Each bar shows only the workspaces living on its own monitor, with one pokeball on that monitor's active workspace. Clean, standard Hyprland behavior, minimal 2-line config change. Bars will show fewer workspace numbers than now.
options.preview:
Monitor 1 bar:  [1]  (pokeball on 1)
Monitor 2 bar:  [2] [3]  (pokeball on 2 or 3)

Each bar = only that monitor's workspaces.
Switching monitors never moves the other bar's ball.

options.label: Keep all 9 on every bar
options.description: Every bar keeps showing all 9 workspace slots AND highlights a different one per monitor. Waybar's native module + CSS cannot do this (CSS is identical across bars); it needs a custom per-output script module rewrite — a much larger change.
options.preview:
Monitor 1 bar:  [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8][9]  (ball on 1)
Monitor 2 bar:  [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8][9]  (ball on 2)

Requires replacing native module with a

content.text:
Good point — and you're right: `hyprctl -j monitors` gives each monitor's `activeWorkspace`, and `hyprctl -j workspaces` gives the workspace→monitor mapping. So the *data* to do this per-monitor is definitely available.

I want to be precise about where the actual blocker is, because it changes the plan:

The data was never the problem — the problem is that the pokeball is a **CSS background image** on Waybar's *native* `hyprland/workspaces` buttons, and Waybar hands **identical CSS classes to both bars**. `.active` = the one globally-focused workspace; `.visible` = workspaces shown on other monitors. Both bars receive the same class info, so pure CSS can't highlight a different button per bar. The only native lever is `all-outputs: false`, which works by *filtering* each bar down to its own monitor's workspaces (hence "only that monitor's" in my earlier question).

To keep **all 9 on every bar AND** highlight a different one per monitor, we have to stop relying on native classes and instead drive it ourselves with a script — which is exactly where your `hyprctl` point comes in. The clean way: **replace the native module with 9 small custom modules** (workspaces 1–9). Each runs a script that reads `$WAYBAR_OUTPUT_NAME` (the bar's monitor), asks `hyprctl` whether that workspace is active *on this monitor*, and emits an `active` class — CSS then paints the **pokeball.png** on it. This is the same pattern your existing `workspace-tabs.sh` already uses (`$WAYBAR_OUTPUT_NAME` + socket2 events). It keeps the real PNG and per-workspace clicking; it's just more moving parts.

So the real choice is complexity vs. completeness:

input.content:
# Per-Monitor Pokeball on Waybar

## Context

The "pokeball" is not a module — it's a CSS background image painted on the
**active** workspace button of the native `hyprland/workspaces` module
(`style.css:30`), using `assets/pokeball.png`.

Today that module has `"all-outputs": true`, so Waybar renders an identical
workspace list on **every** monitor's bar and highlights the single
**globally-focused** workspace on all of them. Result: both monitors' pokeballs
jump together whenever focus moves between monitors.

Goal: each monitor's bar should show the pokeball on **its own** active
workspace, independently. Switching focus/workspaces on one monitor must not
move the other monitor's pokeball.

Chosen approach (confirmed with user): the minimal **native** solution —
`all-outputs: false` so each bar filters to its own monitor's workspaces. Each
bar then shows only that monitor's workspaces, which is accepted.

## Changes

### 1. `/home/krubics/.config/waybar/config.jsonc`

In the `"hyprland/workspaces"` module (lines 27-33), flip:

```jsonc
"all-outputs": false,   // was true
```

This makes each bar instance render only the workspaces on its own monitor

# Per-Monitor Pokeball on Waybar

## Context

The "pokeball" is not a module — it's a CSS background image painted on the
**active** workspace button of the native `hyprland/workspaces` module
(`style.css:30`), using `assets/pokeball.png`.

Today that module has `"all-outputs": true`, so Waybar renders an identical
workspace list on **every** monitor's bar and highlights the single
**globally-focused** workspace on all of them. Result: both monitors' pokeballs
jump together whenever focus moves between monitors.

Goal: each monitor's bar should show the pokeball on **its own** active
workspace, independently. Switching focus/workspaces on one monitor must not
move the other monitor's pokeball.

Chosen approach (confirmed with user): the minimal **native** solution —
`all-outputs: false` so each bar filters to its own monitor's workspaces. Each
bar then shows only that monitor's workspaces, which is accepted.

## Changes

### 1. `/home/krubics/.config/waybar/config.jsonc`

In the `"hyprland/workspaces"` module (lines 27-33), flip:

```jsonc
"all-outputs": false,   // was true
```

This makes each bar instance render only the workspaces on its own monitor
(the bar's `$WAYBAR_OUTPUT_NAME`). The `hyprland/workspaces#taskbar` module
already uses `all-outputs: false`, so this is consistent with existing config.

### 2. `/home/krubics/.config/waybar/style.css`

The pokeball rule (lines 30-44) currently targets only `button.active`. With
`all-outputs: false`:

- The **focused** monitor's bar marks its displayed workspace `.active`.
- A **non-focused** monitor's bar marks its displayed workspace `.visible`
  (Waybar's "visible but not active" class), **not** `.active`.

So targeting only `.active` would leave non-focused monitors with **no**
pokeball. Add `.visible` to the selector so every monitor always shows a
pokeball on its own current workspace:

```css
#workspaces:not(.taskbar) button.active,
#workspaces:not(.taskbar) button.visible {
    /* existing pokeball background rules unchanged */
}
```

No new selectors get contaminated: because `all-outputs: false` filters each
bar to its own monitor's workspaces (and there are no `persistent-workspaces`),
each bar only contains one displayed workspace to mark — so exactly one pokeball
per bar.

## Verification

1. Reload Waybar to pick up config + CSS: `pkill -SIGUSR2 waybar`
   (SIGUSR2 = reload; falls back to `pkill waybar` then relaunch `waybar` if the
   signal reload misbehaves).
2. With workspaces open on both monitors (e.g. ws1 on `eDP-1`, ws3 on
   `HDMI-A-1`), confirm **each** bar shows the pokeball on its own monitor's
   active workspace — cross-check against
   `hyprctl -j monitors | jq '.[] | {name, focused, activeWorkspace: .activeWorkspace.id}'`.
3. Move focus between monitors (mouse or focus bind): the **unfocused** monitor's
   pokeball must stay put; only behavior consistent with each monitor's own
   active workspace should change.
4. Switch the workspace on one monitor (SUPER+N): only **that** monitor's
   pokeball moves; the other monitor's is unaffected.

## Notes / non-goals

- Keeping all 9 workspace numbers on every bar was explicitly declined in favor
  of this minimal approach. If wanted later, it requires replacing the native
  module with per-output custom script modules (hyprctl + `$WAYBAR_OUTPUT_NAME`
  + socket2) — out of scope here.
- No scripts, signals, or intervals are added; the native module + Hyprland's
  socket2 (which Waybar already listens to) drive the updates.
